title: Frog Position After T Seconds
summary: Consider an undirected tree with n vertices numbered 1 to n.
statement: Consider an undirected tree with n vertices numbered 1 to n. A frog initiates at vertex 1 and jumps to an unvisited adjacent vertex each second with equal probability. If no unvisited adjacent vertex exists, the frog remains at its current vertex. Given the edges as pairs of connected vertices, calculate the probability the frog is at the target vertex after t seconds. Results within 0.00001 of the correct answer are acceptable.
constraints: The undirected edges form a tree on vertices one through n, and the frog starts at one.
Each second it chooses uniformly among unvisited neighbors; at a leaf it remains in place.
Return its probability of occupying target after exactly t seconds.
hints: Root the tree implicitly by carrying the parent node.
At a state, divide probability equally among neighbors other than the parent.
Stop at exactly t seconds, or earlier at a leaf because the frog then remains there.
A tree has a unique root-to-node route, so the product of branch probabilities gives the target probability.
editorial: Depth-first probability propagation carries the parent to exclude visited vertices. At a leaf, stopping early is equivalent to remaining there through all later seconds. Otherwise divide by the unvisited child count. The oracle independently advances an explicit probability distribution one second at a time.

tests.explanation: The frog chooses vertex two with probability one third, then vertex four with probability one half, giving one sixth.
With no neighbor, the frog remains at vertex one with probability one.
